title: Anthropic Releases Claude Opus 5
summary: Anthropic released Claude Opus 5, the newest model in its high-end tier.

title: OpenAI Halves the Price of GPT-5.6 Sol
summary: OpenAI cut the price of its GPT-5.

title: An AI Bug-Fixing Tool Was Turned Into a Way In
summary: Security firm Wiz describes how GitHub Copilot's "Autofix" feature — which proposes code fixes automatically — could be manipulated to compromise Snowflake's internal Jira system.

title: A Fake Think Tank Built to Influence Chatbots
summary: Responsible Statecraft reports that Israel set up a think tank that appears to exist mainly so AI chatbots will cite it.

title: A Librarian's Guide to Turning AI Off
summary: Librarian Jessamyn West published a practical list of how to disable or avoid the AI features now switched on by default in search engines, browsers, phones, and office software.

title: Same Machines, 33 Points More Use — Only the Order Changed
summary: A team writing on Hugging Face's blog describes running the same cluster of AI chips 33 percentage points closer to full use without buying anything, purely by changing the order jobs run in.

title: DuckDB Previews Version 2.0
summary: DuckDB published a preview of the highlights coming in version 2.

title: Computer Memory Costs Five Times What It Did a Year Ago
summary: Tom's Hardware reports that memory prices have climbed roughly 500% in twelve months — up to ten times the cheapest levels ever tracked.

title: Apple Changes How Apps Work in the European Union
summary: Apple published a set of changes for apps distributed in the EU.

title: Cursor Launches a GitHub Alternative
summary: Cursor, the AI code editor, has launched Origin — its own service for storing and hosting code, the job GitHub does for most of the software industry.

title: Meta Releases an Open AI Model That Runs on Your Own Machine
summary: Meta published Muse Glimmer, an open source model that handles both text and images, can carry out multi-step tasks, and runs locally instead of in someone else's data centre.

title: A 25-Year-Old Video Patent Expires, Clearing a Problem for Linux
summary: A Brazilian patent covering video technology has run out, ending a long-standing legal complication for Linux.

title: Search That Compares Every Word, Not Just the Whole Document
summary: Sentence Transformers, one of the most widely used open source search libraries, now supports multi-vector — or "late interaction" — models.

title: How Much Memory an AI Agent Needs Depends on How Capable It Already Is
summary: IBM Research tested how much accumulated memory an AI agent actually needs, comparing three configurations across models of different strength.

title: Stripe Is Buying the Place Companies Go to Buy AI
summary: OpenRouter, the service that lets a business reach hundreds of different AI models through one account and one bill, announced it is joining Stripe, the company that processes online payments for a large share of the internet.

title: OpenAI Says It Will Slow Down Where Models Get Good at Hacking
summary: OpenAI published its thinking on how quickly to release models as they become more capable at cyber tasks — the same skills that help defenders find security holes also help attackers exploit them.

title: A Case for Giving AI a Whiteboard Instead of a Chat Window
summary: A GitHub engineer argues that chat is fine for saying what you want but terrible for tracking what an AI assistant actually did — the work disappears up the scroll.

title: Remote Workers Reported the Highest Well-Being in a Study of 7,700 People
summary: Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder surveyed 7,700 employees and found that those working remotely reported better well-being than their on-site counterparts.

title: NVIDIA Releases a Voice Model You Can Run Yourself
summary: NVIDIA published Magpie TTS, a text-to-speech system with open weights, meaning anyone can download it and run it on their own hardware in several languages.

title: Squeezing AI Models Down to Four Bits Without Wrecking Them
summary: Previously covered on 2026-08-13: Liquid AI released LFM2.

title: Go 1.27 Is Out
summary: The Go team shipped version 1.

title: GitHub Explains the August 17 Outage and What It Is Changing
summary: GitHub published an account of the outage that degraded its services on August 17, along with the reliability work it is committing to next.

title: AI Companies Are Cutting Books Apart to Scan Them
summary: Anna's Archive argues that AI companies are buying physical books and destroying them in the process of digitising them, since slicing the spine off is the fastest way to feed pages through a scanner.

title: AliExpress Is Fingerprinting Visitors Through Their Audio Hardware
summary: A developer traced a strange bug in their Bluetooth headphones, which kept dropping the connection to a second device, back to AliExpress running silent audio fingerprinting in the background of its web pages.

title: A Malicious Software Package Ran Its Payload Before Anyone Pressed Run
summary: Security researchers at SafeDep found a package in Rust's public library index that executes hostile code while software is being built, not when it is later run.

title: A Small Model That Plays Piano With You
summary: A developer trained a 125-million-parameter model that autocompletes piano playing and runs entirely on the device rather than in a data centre.

title: Mojo Is Now Open Source
summary: Modular has opened the source code of Mojo, the programming language it built to write high-performance AI code with Python-like syntax.

title: Draft Models That Make Inference Up to 3.2x Faster
summary: Liquid AI released DSpark draft model checkpoints for three models in its LFM2.

title: AI Lifted Homework Scores, Then Exam Scores Fell
summary: The Economist looked at research on students who used AI assistance for their homework.

title: Kagi Will Now Hide Paywalled Pages From Your Search Results
summary: The search engine Kagi added a setting that filters out results you cannot read without paying.

title: A US Traveller Faces Felony Charges for Deleting Data From His Own Phone
summary: The New York Times reports that a man who wiped data from his phone at a US border crossing is now facing felony charges over it.

title: A Voice Model That Starts Talking in Under 50 Milliseconds
summary: Nari Labs published how it cut the delay before a text-to-speech system begins speaking to under 50 milliseconds — fast enough that a spoken reply no longer feels like it is buffering.

title: GitHub Adds a Pane for Keeping Track of What Its AI Is Doing
summary: GitHub's Copilot app now has a "My work" pane that lists every AI session you have running, what is finished, and what is still in progress.

title: Speech Recognition Scores Say Human-Level. The Recordings Disagree.
summary: Hugging Face examined why speech recognition models post near-human accuracy on public benchmarks while still tripping over real recordings.

title: What Happens When You Try to Reproduce 2,200 AI Papers
summary: Hugging Face wrote up what it found running open reproductions of 2,200 papers from ICML, one of the field's main machine learning conferences.

title: A Student Spotted an AI Break-In Attempt and Blew the Whistle
summary: Reuters published an account of how a student in Texas noticed an attempted hack being carried out with an AI system and reported it, setting off the investigation that followed.

title: A Bookmarklet That Drops Any Web Page Into Figma
summary: Figmimic is a one-click bookmarklet that copies a live web page into Figma as editable layers rather than a flat screenshot.

title: A Search Index You Run Yourself
summary: Hister is a full-content search index that stays private and under your control instead of a search company's.

title: GitHub Wants California's AI Transparency Law Amended
summary: GitHub has joined a coalition asking California to make targeted amendments to its AI Transparency Act, arguing that parts of it clash with how open source licensing works.

title: Your Local AI Model Might Be Fine. Your Settings Might Not Be.
summary: A write-up on the Level1Techs forum argues that AI models people run on their own machines often seem worse than they actually are, and that the cause is usually how the model has been set up rather than the model itself.

title: A Rust Language Server That Claims a Hundredth of the Memory
summary: Rust Glancer is a new language server for Rust — the background program your editor talks to for autocomplete, error checking, and jump-to-definition.

title: The Protocol Behind Bluesky Starts Making Room for Private Data
summary: ATProto, the open protocol Bluesky is built on, has published an alpha of "spaces" — an extension that allows records which are not public.

title: Anthropic's Top Claude Tier Is Struggling to Hold Its Users
summary: The Financial Times reports that Anthropic's flagship Claude model — the top-of-the-line tier that competes with OpenAI's most expensive offerings — is having trouble attracting and keeping users, while cheaper AI tools are doing well.

title: Over 170,000 Nonprofits Just Lost All Their Data
summary: Slate investigates how more than 170,000 nonprofit organisations lost every file they had stored with Microsoft, and asks whether the software vendor is responsible.

title: Malware Is Now Infecting the Computer in Your Car's Dashboard
summary: Kaspersky researchers describe malware that infects the Android-based head units used in many modern cars — the screen you use for maps, music, and hands-free calls.

title: Researchers Say They Can Decode Silent Reading From an EEG Cap
summary: A new paper reports decoding what a person is silently reading using only non-invasive EEG — the same kind of stretchy cap used in sleep and brain studies, no implants required.

title: Coconut Oil Jet Fuel Held Its Own Against Kerosene in Engine Tests
summary: StudyFinds reports on engine tests where jet fuel made from coconut oil matched conventional kerosene on efficiency.

title: Someone Rebuilt GPT-2 Using Only CMake
summary: A developer has implemented OpenAI's GPT-2 language model in pure CMake — the tool the software industry normally uses only to describe how to build other programs, not to run them.

title: Hugging Face's Mid-2026 Snapshot of the Open-Model Landscape
summary: Hugging Face published its summer 2026 observations on the state of open AI models — the ones anyone can download, inspect, and run without paying a subscription.

title: Microsoft's Image Apps Are Quietly Tagging the Files You Make
summary: A researcher took apart MS Paint and the Windows Photos app and found they embed an invisible identifier — a unique code known as a GUID — into images you save, including images generated locally on your own machine with no cloud service involved.

title: Thomson Reuters Builds Its Own AI Model
summary: Thomson Reuters, the company behind Westlaw and much of the legal and tax research industry, has launched a frontier AI model of its own, trained on its data holdings rather than licensing someone else's system.

title: Apple Keeps Hide My Email on iCloud.com
summary: Apple confirmed that iCloud+ Hide My Email addresses — the disposable addresses you can hand to a website instead of your real one — will keep using icloud.

title: Your Alt Text Can Pass the Checker and Still Be Useless
summary: GitHub built a plugin for its accessibility scanner that judges whether image descriptions actually describe anything, rather than just confirming that some text exists.

title: Researchers Measure AI Agents Flooding Government Services
summary: A new paper documents what happens when automated AI agents submit requests to public services at machine speed — forms, applications and enquiries arriving faster than any human queue was designed for.

title: Gradio Adds Wire-It-Together AI Workflows
summary: Gradio, the open source toolkit most commonly used to put a web interface on a machine learning model, now supports chaining steps into a workflow: generate an image, cut out its background, run it through another model, all as one pipeline.

title: An Argument That Models Could Escape Through the Software Running Them
summary: An essay makes the case that the risk in running a large language model is not only what the model says, but the program serving it.
